title: Given an array of elements, return the k elements that appear most frequently, using a hash map to count and a heap to select.
shortTitle: Find the Top K Frequent Elements

s1_definition.profdef: Finding the top k frequent elements means returning the k values with the highest occurrence counts. The standard approach counts occurrences with a hash map, then selects the k highest counts, typically with a size-k min-heap keyed by frequency so the least frequent of the current top k sits at the root for cheap eviction. Counting is linear, and heap selection over m distinct values is m log k.
s1_definition.analogy: Imagine the National Bank of India wants the three most common merchant categories customers spend on. A clerk first tallies every transaction into a count sheet, one running count per category. Then she keeps a small tray holding only the three categories with the biggest counts so far, arranged so the smallest count is at the front. For each category's final count, if it beats the front of the tray she swaps it in. At the end the tray holds the three most frequent categories, and she never had to fully sort every category.
s1_definition.oneliner: Count with a hash map, then keep the k highest counts in a size-k min-heap keyed by frequency.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding the top k frequent elements means returning the k values with the highest occurrence counts. The standard approach counts occurrences with a hash map, then selects the k highest counts, typically with a size-k min-heap keyed by frequency so the least frequent of the current top k sits at the root for cheap eviction. Counting is linear, and heap selection over m distinct values is m log k.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** Imagine the National Bank of India wants the three most common merchant categories customers spend on. A clerk first tallies every transaction into a count sheet, one running count per category. Then she keeps a small tray holding only the three categories with the biggest counts so far, arranged so the smallest count is at the front. For each category's final count, if it beats the front of the tray she swaps it in. At the end the tray holds the three most frequent categories, and she never had to fully sort every category.

**One line to remember:** Count with a hash map, then keep the k highest counts in a size-k min-heap keyed by frequency.

sections.s2_technical:
The problem splits into two phases: counting and selecting. Counting is a single pass that builds a frequency map, for example `counts.merge(element, 1, Integer::sum)`, which adds one to the running count for each element, creating the entry if absent. After this pass the map holds each distinct element mapped to how many times it occurred.

Selection is where the heap helps. You want the k entries with the largest counts. A size-k min-heap ordered by count keeps exactly the current top k: you offer each map entry, and if the heap exceeds k you poll, which removes the entry with the smallest count. Because the heap is a min-heap by frequency, the root is always the weakest of the current leaders, so evicting it is correct. For example `PriorityQueue<Map.Entry<E,Integer>> heap = new PriorityQueue<>(Comparator.comparingInt(Map.Entry::getValue));`. After processing all distinct entries, the heap holds the top k by frequency.

Counting is linear in the total number of elements n, and selection is m log k where m is the number of distinct elements, so the whole thing is n plus m log k. That beats fully sorting all distinct elements by frequency, which would be m log m, whenever k is smaller than m, which is the usual case.

A senior-level nuance is bucket sort by frequency, which achieves linear time overall. Since any count is between one and n, you create n-plus-one buckets indexed by frequency, drop each element into its count bucket, then walk buckets from high to low collecting k elements. That is O(n) with no heap, trading a bit of extra memory. I present the heap solution as the clean general answer and mention bucket sort as the linear-time optimisation when counts are bounded.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India wants to know the most common merchant categories its customers transact in, to design targeted offers, from a large stream of categorised transactions. We need the top few categories by count, not a full ranking. This is exactly top-k frequent, counting then selecting.

Problem 2 — There can be many distinct categories, so after counting we do not want to sort them all; we only want the top k, and we want selection cost to depend on k, not on the full number of categories. A size-k min-heap keyed by frequency gives exactly that.

In our mini-project we build a `CategoryAnalytics` service that returns the top k categories by transaction count using a frequency map plus a frequency-ordered PriorityQueue. The demo feeds a list of category codes and asks for the top two.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: the category codes grocery, fuel, grocery, dining, grocery, fuel, dining, grocery, fuel, travel, asking for the top two.

Step 1: We count in one pass. Grocery occurs four times, fuel three times, dining two times, travel once. The frequency map now holds these four counts.

Step 2: We build a min-heap keyed by count. We offer grocery with four. Heap holds grocery. We offer fuel with three. Heap holds fuel then grocery, with fuel smaller at the root.

Step 3: We offer dining with two. The heap size becomes three, exceeding k of two, so we poll the smallest count, which is dining with two, and evict it. The heap holds fuel three and grocery four.

Step 4: We offer travel with one. Size three again, poll the smallest, which is travel with one, and evict it. The heap holds fuel three and grocery four.

Step 5: All distinct categories processed. The heap holds the two most frequent, fuel and grocery, with fuel at the root because its count is smaller.

Step 6: We extract by polling and inserting at the front, so the final highest-first order is grocery with four then fuel with three. We never sorted all four categories fully; selection depended only on k.

```
  ┌─ Design Patterns Used ───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │  Two-phase: frequency map (count) then bounded min-heap       │
  │  Comparator by frequency for selection                        │

  │  S: CategoryAnalytics only computes top-k frequent            │

  ┌───────────────────────────────────────┐
  │           CategoryAnalytics           │
  │  ──────────────────────────────────── │
  │  + topKFrequent(elements, k): List    │  O(n + m log k)
  └───────────────────────────────────────┘
      Pre:  k ≤ number of distinct elements
      Post: k most frequent, highest-first

  ── State Diagram: Selection ─────────────────────────────

  [count phase] → frequency map
  [offer entry] → heap; size>k → poll least frequent
  [extract] → poll all, reverse → highest-first

  ── Call Chain ────────────────────────────────────────────

  1. topKFrequent(elements, k)
  2.   for each e: counts.merge(e,1,sum)
  3.   for each entry: heap.offer; if size>k → poll
  4.   drain heap addFirst → return
```
sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the top k frequent elements means returning the k values that appear most often, and I split it into two phases. First I count occurrences in a single linear pass using a hash map, where for each element I add one to its running count, creating the entry if it is new. After that pass the map holds every distinct value mapped to how many times it appeared.

Then I select the k highest counts with a size-k min-heap keyed by frequency. I offer each map entry into the heap, and whenever the heap grows beyond k I poll once, which removes the entry with the smallest count. Because it is a min-heap by frequency, the root is always the weakest of the current leaders, so evicting it is exactly right. After processing all distinct entries the heap holds the top k, and I drain it, reversing the order so the most frequent comes first. Counting is linear in n and selection is m log k over m distinct values, so the whole thing is n plus m log k, which beats fully sorting all distinct values whenever k is smaller than m.

In my banking project at the National Bank of India I used this to find the most common merchant categories customers transact in, to feed a targeted-offers engine. There can be many distinct categories, so I did not want to sort them all; the heap kept selection cost tied to k rather than to the full number of categories.

The senior-level point I make is that when counts are bounded, which they always are because any count is between one and n, there is a linear-time alternative called bucket sort by frequency. I create n-plus-one buckets indexed by count, drop each element into its count bucket, then walk the buckets from highest frequency down, collecting k elements. That is O(n) with no heap at all, trading a little extra memory for speed. So I present the heap solution as the clean general answer and name bucket sort as the linear optimisation when I want to squeeze out the log factor.
